column4: The section's riya (showing-off) meets spending made for people to see: the smooth rock's dust is washed away by rain, and the spenders cannot command anything of what they earned. Its “cannot measure/control” link is the same root q-d-r as 90:5.
The section links the bound man with his failure to urge food for the poor; this ayah supplies that precise failure, “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ.”
The section's left-side figure is the man given his record in his left hand, “بِشِمَالِهِۦ”; this starts the same judgment scene that binds his neck and exposes his neglect of the poor.
The section's speaker who says he spent much wealth meets this man's confession that his wealth did not avail him, “مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ.”
The section explicitly connects its “I spent” with “my power has perished”; the ayah's “هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَٰنِيَهْ” states the loss of the power he presumed.
The left-handed figure's punishment proceeds to restraint: “خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ” seizes and fetters the same man whose neck the section says is bound.
This next step in the same judgment scene orders him into the Fire, completing the section's movement from bound neck to sealed fire.
The chain extending seventy cubits gives a concrete binding of the neck that the section places beside release of a neck.
The neighboring ayah names the man's disbelief in God as part of the same sequence, linking the left-side outcome to the section's sign-deniers.
The oath-expiration here joins feeding ten poor people with freeing a neck, the very two acts the section says the Quran places together when an oath is expiated.
The garden owners swear to harvest early; the section sets their oath against the city oath that opens toward feeding its poor.
Their oath excludes even an exception (“وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ”), making the binding of an oath serve the reverse purpose from the section's release and feeding.
The owners' whispered rule, “لَا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ... مِسْكِينٌ,” directly reverses the section's feeding of the hungry and poor.
The section names the root wāw-ṣād-dāl in 90:20; here the cave dog's “بِٱلْوَصِيدِ” (at the threshold) meets sleepers turned to the right and left in one scene.
Moses sees fire while traveling and hopes to find “عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ هُدًۭى”; the section contrasts that guiding fire with the fire sealed over the way's end.
Moses again sees fire during travel and hopes for news or a brand from it; this repeated wayfarer's fire helps mark the reversal to a fire no longer serving as a sign.
In another telling of Moses' journey, “ءَانَسْتُ نَارًۭا” begins a search for news or a burning brand, a traveling fire opposite the sealed destination-fire.
The section quotes the crowd “مُّقْتَحِمٌۭ” rushing in with the condemned; it is the image of plunging into fire opposite the unentered uphill passage.

The section quotes the same root ṣ-b-r in the astonished phrase “فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ”: endurance here is a doomed daring to face fire, divided from the self-restraint needed on the ascent.
The section identifies the root wāw-ṣād-dāl as closing; this ayah uses “مُّؤْصَدَةٌ” for the Fire shut over its people, a direct counterpart to 90:20.
The next ayah says the shut Fire is in extended columns, completing the enclosure that the section's closed-fire image evokes.
The section explicitly recalls the man who could have been raised by signs but “أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ”; this is its clearest image of sticking to the low ground instead of rising by the passage.
This creation scene says the human is tested and given hearing and sight, setting up the section's created person endowed with eyes and directed toward a moral choice.
“هَدَيْنَٰهُ ٱلسَّبِيلَ” states that the path is shown and the human may be grateful or ungrateful, a direct parallel to the two ways in the section.
The same sequence moves from guidance to chains, shackles, and blazing fire for deniers, joining the section's shown path to the closed-fire boundary.
This account of righteousness joins freeing a neck, giving wealth to orphan and poor, and patience in adversity; it gathers the section's passage acts into one moral scene.
The section joins city and hunger through the dictionary gloss “orphan in famine”; this ayah names the city-feeding counterpart, “أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍۢ,” and security from fear.
The section's people who adhere like plants meet the crop here: it puts forth shoots, strengthens them, and grows firm, an image of connected growth.
The section's mutual compassion “as if from the same womb” meets the ayah's one-soul origin and its explicit “وَٱلْأَرْحَامَ” (wombs), grounding kinship in shared origin.
The human is created and “فَقَدَّرَهُۥ” (measured/shaped); this is a close formulation of the section's sequence from creation through measure.
The section says Quran joins measuring and guidance in its order; “قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ” states that exact measure-then-guidance sequence.
Against the section's person who thinks no one sees him, this warning asks whether he knows that God sees, “بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ.”
The section's self-assured man thinks no one can master him; this passage says the human transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, naming the same false independence.
This adjoining ayah identifies the conceit—“أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ”—that makes the section's imagined immunity from power and sight possible.
The section places eyes beside the claim of being unseen; this ayah says God knows “خَآئِنَةَ ٱلْأَعْيُنِ” and what hearts conceal, closing that imagined privacy.
The section's bound-neck and unseen person meet the statement that God is nearer than “حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ”; the hidden self is known even at the neck's life-line.
This passage asks why the orphan is not honored, the reverse of the section's call to meet the passage by caring for a related orphan.
“وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ” directly repeats the failure to urge feeding the poor that the section joins to the bound man's fate.
The section's amassed wealth and neglected hungry person meet the denunciation of loving wealth with excessive love, showing the inward attachment behind withholding.
The denier of judgment “يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ” (repels the orphan), a direct reversal of the section's demanded care for the orphan.
This ayah condemns failing to urge feeding the needy, matching the section's repeated link between an un-fed poor person and failed passage.
The righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive together; this closely stages the section's hungry mouth, orphan, poor person, and released neck.
The speaker recalls finding the addressee an orphan and sheltering him, a direct orphan-and-protection scene for the section's kinless child.
The same address recalls finding the addressee needy and enriching him, meeting the section's transition from hunger to provision.
The command not to undo oaths after confirming them meets the section's image of oaths knotted and then expiated through release and feeding.
The spun thread undone after being firm gives a specific reversal for the section's bound-and-released sequence of oath and neck.
Against 2:264's showy gift washed off bare stone, this neighboring spend is likened to a garden on high ground whose rain yields fruit; it shows giving that remains fruitful.
The seed multiplied into many ears is a concrete counter-image to the section's expenditure that leaves no gain, showing charity's yield rather than its erasure.
The section's root and wording for riya (showing-off) recur in spending wealth to be seen by people, a direct lexical parallel to the false display in 2:264.
The human is described as laboring arduously toward the Lord until meeting Him, giving the section's created hardship a path and destination.
The promise that ease accompanies hardship speaks directly to the section's human created amid toil and its difficult ascent.
This repeated promise confirms that the arduous passage is accompanied by ease, not a closed end.
Joseph's interpretation of seven harsh years consuming what was stored gives a concrete extended famine alongside the section's day of hunger.
The next year of relief, rain, and pressing produce completes the famine sequence with a specific return of provision after scarcity.
The example of a secure, provisioned city made to taste hunger and fear reverses the city that the section says is fed from hunger and secured from fear.
The next step after human creation and measure says “ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ,” the path was made easy, completing a creation-to-way sequence.
Moses answers Pharaoh that the Lord gave each thing its form and then guided it, another explicit creation-and-guidance formulation behind the section's sequence.
The arrogant walker cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height; this boundary reverses the section's ascent, which is achieved by bending toward those on the ground.
In the separate zihar-expiration setting, return requires freeing a neck before the spouses touch; this repeats the section's release-of-a-neck act.
The next ayah requires feeding sixty poor people when that release is impossible, connecting release and feeding in a different expiation sequence.
As a neighbor to Moses' fire in 27:7, the scene turns the travel-fire into a blessed divine encounter, completing the image of a fire that guides.
The neighboring continuation of 28:29 places the call at the blessed tree on the valley's right side; the fire-lit journey opens into guidance rather than enclosure.
The next account gives him no food except “غِسْلِينٍۢ”; after the section's cited failure to feed the poor, this is the specific food of the condemned man.
The neighbor identifies that foul food as reserved for wrongdoers, completing the reversal between withholding food from the poor and one's own final ration.
Their spending is likened to a freezing wind striking a crop and destroying it; this parallels the section's rain washing away the dust of a showy gift.
The root r-y-ʾ appears here in “يُرَآءُونَ” for people who show off their prayer; it extends the section's public display from spending to worship.
The showy worshipers then withhold even small aid, a pointed reversal of the section's visible performance versus feeding and mercy.
The feeders say they act only for God's face and seek no thanks; that motive contrasts with the section's gift made for people to see.
The command not to repel the asker carries the same concrete compassion as the section's feeding of one in need.
The passage names fear, hunger, and loss of wealth as trials and gives glad tidings to the patient, connecting the section's famine-day passage with sabr under hardship.
Believers are called siblings and told to reconcile; this gives the section's people who pity one another as if from one womb a concrete communal counterpart.
The people become brothers after God joins their hearts; this supplies a specific image for the section's compassion binding people together.
Believing men and women are each other's allies and mutually uphold good; this parallels the section's repeated mutual urging of patience and mercy.
The enemy group seems gathered, yet its hearts are divided; this reverses the section's plants adhering and community made tender by shared kinship.
The preceding ayah says God created and formed; with 87:3 it supplies the creation step in the section's create-measure-guide sequence.
The preceding ayah asks what the human was created from, opening the same human creation-to-measure-to-path sequence.
The companions of the right name the same right-side company as 90:18, giving the section's right-hand outcome a repeated Quranic formulation.
The companions of the left provide the matching left-side boundary to the section's contrast between the two companies.
This next description develops the companions of the right as a distinct saved group, completing the side label in 56:8.
This next description develops the companions of the left amid heat and smoke, linking the side label in 56:9 with the section's fire-bound end.
The day each community is called with its record, those given the record in their right hands, gives the section's right-side company a judgment-scene counterpart to the left-hand record in 69:25.
The section's word lubad for amassed wealth meets this ayah's collecting and counting of wealth; it makes the piled-up property a sign of false security.
The wealth-collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal, sharpening the section's portrait of a man who assumes no one can overpower him.
The section's source word lubad for amassed wealth shares root l-b-d with “لِبَدًا,” a tightly packed crowd around the servant; the pile-image shifts from property to people pressing close.
In the fasting passage, feeding a poor person appears as a provision when one cannot fast; it concretely joins bodily hunger and feeding the needy, though in a different legal setting.
This passage opens a direct two-path parallel: the one who gives and is mindful follows the charitable ascent that the section sets against refusing the passage.
The giver's affirmation of the good completes the first path's stance, corresponding to the section's faith and mutual counsel alongside mercy.
The giver is made at ease for ease; this explicitly casts moral choice as a way made passable, echoing the section's guided ways and difficult ascent.
The opposite person is miserly and thinks himself self-sufficient, directly meeting the section's wealthy man who assumes he cannot be overcome.
The second path rejects the good, a specific counterpart to refusing the section's passage of release and feeding.
The withholding person is made at ease for hardship, turning the section's unentered uphill path toward its opposite outcome.
The ayah says wealth will not avail its owner at the fall, a direct outcome for the self-assured spender whose wealth the section links to vanished power.
The declaration that guidance belongs to God meets the section's two guided ways and contrasts guidance with human claims of control.
The warning of a blazing fire gives the rejected path the same fiery endpoint that the section contrasts with a fire used as a guide.
This ayah specifies who enters that fire, helping define the boundary between the two sides of the section's image.
The fire-bound person is described as denying and turning away, a compact parallel to the section's deniers of signs who refuse the passage.
The other path is kept away from the fire, giving the section's right-side people a clear counterpart to its fire-enclosed side.
The God-conscious person gives wealth to purify himself, directly joining the section's spending, care for the poor, and upward moral movement.
The gift is not repayment for a favor owed, clarifying a motive opposite the section's display for people to see.
The giver seeks the face of the Most High Lord, specifying the inward audience that replaces the section's ostentatious giving for people.
The closing assurance of satisfaction completes this giving path's outcome, beside the section's right-side destination.
The announced blazing Fire is an explicit counterpart to the section's sealed Fire at the end of the refused way.
The Fire calls those who turned away, a concrete joining of refusal and fiery destination like the section's unentered passage and covered signs.
The same passage identifies the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it, joining refusal of the way to the wealth that the section says cannot save.
The human is described as created anxious, a close formulation of the section's human created amid hardship and its uphill trial.
When hardship touches him, he is impatient, specifying the panic against which the section says sabr on the ascent must hold.
When good reaches him, he withholds it; this concretely reverses the section's feeding of the hungry and release of the bound.
The righteous keep a known share in their wealth, making the section's act of spending for the needy a standing right rather than display.
The next ayah names the share's recipients as the asker and deprived, directly meeting the section's poor and hungry mouth.
Belief in the Day of Recompense supplies the judgmental setting for the wealth-share just named, like the section's right and left outcomes.
Those who fear their Lord's punishment give a specific stance that accords with the section's patience and mercy before its fire boundary.
The declaration that no one is secure from punishment reverses the section's arrogant assumption that no one can overpower him.
The cave companions send one with their silver into the city to obtain food; this next step after 18:18 connects the threshold scene with the section's city and feeding images.
Abraham asks for this city to be made secure and its people supplied with fruits, a concrete parallel to the section's city fed from hunger and protected from fear.
Abraham settles descendants by the Sacred House in a barren valley and asks for provision; it joins the section's city, lineage, and need for food in one scene.
The secure sanctuary stands amid people seized around it; this supplies another specific city-and-safety formulation beside the section's city fed and made secure.
The oath by the secure city repeats the section's opening oath on the city, adding security as the city's stated quality.
The next ayah says the human was created in the best form, adding a human-creation formulation to the section's created person and faculties.
The human can be brought to the lowest low, a direct vertical reversal of the section's ascent and its person who clings to earth.
Believers who do good deeds are excepted and receive an unfailing reward, specifying how the descent is reversed by the section's charitable way.
This closing ayah explicitly joins faith and good works with mutual counsel to truth and patience, repeating one of the section's named acts and its collective form.
The command to lower the wing of humility out of mercy to one's parents gives an exact downward motion for the section's claim that ascent comes by stooping in compassion.
Severing kinship ties is condemned, a specific reversal of the section's community that pities one another as though from one womb.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each accountable, connecting the section's gifted faculties and the illusion of being unseen to judgment for their use.
On the Day of Witness, tongues and hands testify to what people did; this makes the section's given tongue and its hidden actions publicly answerable.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify, turning the section's fear of being unseen into bodily evidence at judgment.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their owners, a specific answer to the section's person who thinks no one sees him.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are promised fire in their bellies and a blaze, joining the section's orphan, wealth, and fiery consequence in one warning.

This command joins protecting orphan wealth, giving full measure, speaking justly even about kin, and fulfilling a covenant; it gathers the section's orphan, measure, relation, and oath motifs in one ayah.
The command not to approach an orphan's property except rightly, followed by fulfilling covenants, joins the section's vulnerable orphan with its oath-bound moral responsibility.
The ayah says that if people mix their affairs with orphans, they are their brothers; this makes explicit the kin-like bond behind the section's orphan and same-womb compassion.
The answer about what to spend names parents, near kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, directly collecting the section's relational beneficiaries into a giving scene.
The command to give the near relative, needy person, and traveler their due makes the section's kinship and feeding acts concrete duties.
This command lists parents, kin, orphan, needy, neighbor, traveler, and those in bondage as recipients of good treatment, closely matching the section's web of care and release.
The helpers prefer others over themselves even when in need and are protected from miserliness, giving a specific communal counterpart to the section's feeding and mutual mercy.
The person given his record in the right hand receives an easy account, a judgment counterpart to the section's right-side company.
The person given his record from behind his back meets the section's left-side boundary in a contrasting judgment image.
The next ayah says that he will enter a blazing fire, completing the fire consequence of the preceding back-handed record.
Those who spend without following their gift with reminders or injury receive a reward; this neighboring passage supplies the ethical opposite of the section's showy spending.
A kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury, sharpening the section's contrast between public display and actual mercy.
Secret charity is better, though open charity is also good; this directly answers the section's spend-for-people-to-see image.
Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, receive reward and fear no grief; it gives a specific faithful counterpart to ostentatious spending.
The ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, making expenditure a threshold to goodness like the section's passage.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend in God's way face painful punishment, directly tying withheld wealth to the section's refusal and fire.
The hoarded metal is heated in the Fire and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, giving a bodily fire consequence to the section's wealth-and-fire conjunction.
The hand is pictured chained to the neck for miserliness and then overextended in spending; this meets the section's neck-release image and the boast of having spent much wealth.
The faithful neither spend extravagantly nor withhold but keep a middle course, a specific counterpoint to the boast of lavish spending without mercy.
The abundant provision makes a person claim honor, opening the same sequence that corrects him for failing to honor the orphan.
When provision is restricted the person claims humiliation; this clarifies the section's hunger and counters treating material measure as a person's worth.
The same people consume inheritance greedily, a specific misuse of wealth against the orphan and kinship that the section calls into mercy.
The gatherer of wealth is cast into the Crusher, beginning a punishment sequence that ends in the shut Fire linked by the section to its closing image.
This ayah asks what the Crusher is, extending the same wealth-and-fire warning toward its explicit fire description.
The Crusher is described as God's kindled fire, a neighboring specification of the fire shut over people in 104:8.
The fire reaches the hearts, adding its inward effect to the closed-fire scene the section links with denied signs.
The expiation for accidental killing includes freeing a believing neck, a separate legal setting that repeats the section's concrete act of releasing a neck.
The ayah warns not to use oaths as a barrier to righteousness, piety, or making peace; it makes the section's oath-and-passage meeting explicit.
The Creator is said to have created everything and determined it with exact measure, another direct creation-and-measure formulation behind the section's sequence.
Everything is created according to measure, a repeated formulation for the section's measurement motif and the human claim about power.
Deeds are weighed, connecting the section's measure/capacity language to the judgment that sorts people by what they have done.
The next ayah gives the heavy-scale person a pleasing life, completing one measured outcome beside the section's right-side company.
The light-scale person supplies the opposite result to the section's right-side path.
The next ayah names the light-scale person's destination as the abyss, completing the adverse measured outcome.
This ayah asks what the abyss is, continuing the measured-judgment scene.
The abyss is specified as a blazing fire, joining measured deeds to the section's fire-bound side.
Those whose scales are heavy are successful; this makes measure determine an outcome like the section's division into right and left companies.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell, completing the contrary measured outcome with a fire destination.
Anyone who has done an atom's weight of good will see it, directly countering the section's assumption that no one sees and making small deeds visible.
The same rule makes even an atom's weight of evil visible, giving the section's unseen person an exact boundary at judgment.
